sourceParagraphs.0: NRBS 4210: Nursing Practice of the Adult Client III
sourceParagraphs.2: Know the NURSING PROCESS and how to apply the nursing process to all disease processes.Know the risk factors, clinical manifestations, signs & symptoms, medical management,pharmacological and non-pharmacological therapies, side effects of therapy, nutrition, nursingassessment, management, and nursing diagnoses. Know what the nurse should prioritize, nursefirst action, plan of care, interventions, and evaluation for all of the following diagnoses plus thespecifics under each umbrella.
sourceParagraphs.3: All of the above statements apply to each bullet and then the extra bullets are some highlights inthat are in that area
sourceParagraphs.7: Two major Parkinson subtypes are tremor and non-tremor dominant
sourceParagraphs.9: Present in the majority of patients at diagnosis
sourceParagraphs.10: Disappears with purposeful movement and during sleep
sourceParagraphs.11: Rhythmic, slow turning motion of the forearm and hand
sourceParagraphs.12: Motion of the thumb against the fingers as if rolling a pill
sourceParagraphs.16: Involuntary stiffness increases with voluntary active movement
sourceParagraphs.18: Bradykinesia: Overall slowing of active movement and speech
sourceParagraphs.19: Patients take longer to complete activities
sourceParagraphs.20: Akinesia: Difficulty initiating movement, rising from a sitting position, turning in bed
sourceParagraphs.22: Propulsive gait: leaning forward, shuffling gait, stooped over.
sourceParagraphs.23: Loss of postural reflexes: inability to maintain equilibrium and recover balance when displaced by a unexpected movement.
sourceParagraphs.24: Forward flexion of the neck, hips, knees, and elbows
sourceParagraphs.28: Positive response to levodopa trial confirms diagnosis
sourceParagraphs.29: Most effective agent, converted to dopamine in the basal ganglia
sourceParagraphs.30: Often combined with carbidopa, which protects the levodopa from breakdown in the bloodstream.
sourceParagraphs.31: Adverse effects: Dyskinesia, nausea, vomiting, decreased BP, confusion
sourceParagraphs.32: On-off syndrome: Sudden periods of near immobility followed by return of medication effectiveness
sourceParagraphs.34: High risk for aspiration pneumonia in Parkinson’s patients
sourceParagraphs.36: Semisolid diet with thick liquids easier to swallow. Avoid thin liquids.
sourceParagraphs.38: Place food on tongue, close lips and teeth, lift tongue up and back, swallow.
sourceParagraphs.40: Hold head upright, make conscious effort to swallow.
sourceParagraphs.42: Controlling symptoms and maintaining functional independence.
sourceParagraphs.43: Nutritional intake may be impaired by functional disability/decrease
sourceParagraphs.45: Impaired bowel and bladder elimination caused by muscle weakness
sourceParagraphs.48: An autoimmune neuromuscular disorder that attacks the neuromuscular junction. Antibodies block or destroy acetylcholine receptors where nerves meet skeletal muscles, preventing proper muscle activation
sourceParagraphs.50: Hallmark: muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest
sourceParagraphs.51: Ocular (most common): ptosis, diplopia; ptosis or diplopia often appears first
sourceParagraphs.54: Respiratory: dyspnea, weak cough, myasthenic crisis
sourceParagraphs.55: Ice pack test: ice on a drooping eyelid for 2 to 5 minutes; if the eyelid lifts it supports MG
sourceParagraphs.57: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors relieve symptoms only and do not change the disease course
sourceParagraphs.59: Timing: give pyridostigmine 30-60 minutes before meals to optimize chewing/swallowing and reduce aspiration risk
sourceParagraphs.60: Works quickly and wears off quickly - take it about 30-60 minutes before meals or demanding activities
sourceParagraphs.64: Cholinergic crisis: too much medication -> give atropine and benzodiazepines
sourceParagraphs.65: Both cause weakness with trouble breathing and swallowing
sourceParagraphs.68: An immune-mediated disease that attacks the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord). It destroys the protective covering around nerve fibers called the myelin sheath, disrupting brain-to-body communication.
sourceParagraphs.70: Manifestations can relapse and remiss or be progressively declining
sourceParagraphs.71: Vision changes (sudden decrease/loss, blurred, double vision)
sourceParagraphs.72: Numbness, tingling, or sensory loss in body or limbs
sourceParagraphs.75: Fatigue, weakness in arms or legs
sourceParagraphs.76: Pain: patients may need daily analgesics
sourceParagraphs.77: Heat sensitivity (which may trigger the above)
sourceParagraphs.78: Uhthoff phenomenon: a temporary worsening of neurological symptoms in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) when core body temperature rises
sourceParagraphs.80: Lumbar puncture: Have patient lie down for at least 30 minutes after LP and educate them to drink a lot of fluid for at least 24 hours after
sourceParagraphs.81: MRI can sometimes show myelin plaques
sourceParagraphs.83: Neurodegenerative disease of unknown cause involving loss of motor neurons in the spinal cord and brain stem
sourceParagraphs.84: Diagnosed based on signs and symptoms
sourceParagraphs.88: Progressive fasciculations: small, involuntary muscle twitching
sourceParagraphs.92: Assess swallowing and risk for aspiration
sourceParagraphs.103: Increased ICP: Cushing’s Triad -> HTN, Bradycardia, Tachypnea
sourceParagraphs.104: Droplet precaution during the first 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy for meningococcal meningitis; close contacts may require prophylactic antibiotics
sourceParagraphs.107: FIRST step is blood cultureabx immediately
sourceParagraphs.108: NEVER withhold or delay antibiotics for CT or LP
sourceParagraphs.110: Lie supine for at least an hour and encourage fluids
sourceParagraphs.111: Post-LP headache managed with caffeine, laying down, analgesics
sourceParagraphs.112: Bacterial vs Viral Meningitis LP results:
sourceParagraphs.113: Both have increased leukocyte and neutrophils in CSF
sourceParagraphs.114: Bacterial: CSF has elevated protein and low glucose levels
sourceParagraphs.115: Viral: CSF has normal protein and normal glucose levels
sourceParagraphs.117: Immune system attacks peripheral nerve myelin.
sourceParagraphs.122: Treatment IVIG or sometimes TPE (plasma exchange)
sourceParagraphs.124: IVIG nursing: baseline VS, lung sounds, fluid status. Start slowly, then increase. Watch for anaphylaxis, headache, aseptic meningitis, renal failure, fluid overload.
sourceParagraphs.125: Plasma exchange nursing: watch for hypotension and citrate-induced hypocalcemia (perioral/finger tingling, cramps → IV calcium). Recheck platelets, fibrinogen, and electrolytes.
sourceParagraphs.130: Symmetric pain, swelling, warmth in small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists, feet) → later knees, shoulders, cervical spine,TMJ.
sourceParagraphs.131: Morning stiffness > 1 hour. Pain ↑ with rest, ↓ with activity. Joints feel "boggy" or spongy
sourceParagraphs.135: Only drugs that stop joint destruction
sourceParagraphs.136: Start early, most joint destruction is in the first 12 weeks and they take 6 weeks to work
sourceParagraphs.137: Utilize low dose steroid bridge in the meantime
sourceParagraphs.138: Methotrexate first, given weekly (or leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine)
sourceParagraphs.140: Fever/infection on a DMARD or biologic → hold the dose and notify the provider
sourceParagraphs.147: Cartilage breaks down → osteophytes (bone spurs), narrowed joint space
sourceParagraphs.149: Pain worse with activity, better with rest
sourceParagraphs.150: Asymmetric in weight bearing joins such as knees and hips
sourceParagraphs.151: Heberden (Distal Interphalangeal joint), Bouchard (Proximal Interphalangeal joint) nodes,
sourceParagraphs.156: Low-impact exercise to help with mobility
sourceParagraphs.157: Steroid join injections a few times per year
sourceParagraphs.158: Joint replacement when conservative treatment fails
sourceParagraphs.160: Patho: Bone breakdown is greater than bone building leading to porous, brittle bone.
sourceParagraphs.162: Bone loss speeds up in the first 5 years after menopause.
sourceParagraphs.163: S/S: kyphosis, height loss, fracture is often first sign
sourceParagraphs.165: Calcium-rich diet: 1,000–1,300 mg/day (teens/young adults); ~1,200 mg for postmenopausal women and older adults
sourceParagraphs.171: Screen all women over 65 and women under 65 with risk factors as well as men over 70
sourceParagraphs.172: Before scan hold calcium supplements for 24h
sourceParagraphs.179: Sudden attack, often at NIGHT: severe pain, red, hot, swollen joint.
sourceParagraphs.180: 1 site: great toe (1st MTP joint). Also ankle and knee. Usually one joint at a time.
sourceParagraphs.181: Triggers: alcohol, big meal/red meat, trauma, surgery, illness, dieting, diuretics.
sourceParagraphs.182: Diet: caused by diet high in purines
sourceParagraphs.183: Limit purines in the diet; organ meats, red meat, shellfish
sourceParagraphs.184: Drink lots of water to flush out uric acid
sourceParagraphs.186: Allopurinol is first line against uric acid production
sourceParagraphs.191: Episodic VERTIGO (most troublesome; lasts 20 min–12 h)
sourceParagraphs.193: FLUCTUATING SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS (starts with low frequencies, progressive)
sourceParagraphs.195: Diagnosis (no single test): ≥2 vertigo attacks + hearing loss on audiogram + other causes ruled out (MRI for acoustic neuroma).
sourceParagraphs.196: Weber test: sound louder in the unaffected (good) ear (sensorineural loss).
sourceParagraphs.197: Romberg: sway with eyes closed (stay close; don't do it during an acute attack).
sourceParagraphs.198: Hydrochlorothiazide is used to lower body fluid and thus endolymph fluid
sourceParagraphs.202: Obesity (postmenopausal), alcohol, smoking, inactivity, not breastfeeding
sourceParagraphs.204: Teach: blue-green urine/stool (and skin tint) for ~24 h from the dye..
sourceParagraphs.205: Monitor the injection site. Assess the arm for early lymphedema.
sourceParagraphs.206: Possible seroma (pocket of fluid beneath skin), numbness/neuropathic sensations, ↓ arm mobility → ROM exercises.
sourceParagraphs.207: Final pathology can still be positive (frozen-section false negatives) → may still need axillary lymph node dissection
sourceParagraphs.208: SLNB vs. ALND: SLNB is outpatient, 15–30 min, no drain, minimal lymphedema risk, less ROM loss. ALND = general anesthesia, drain, higher lymphedema risk.
sourceParagraphs.212: Ages 30–65: HPV + Pap co-test every 5 yr
sourceParagraphs.215: Abnormal/irregular uterine bleeding at any age
sourceParagraphs.216: Thickened endometrium on transvaginal ultrasound (postmenopausal lining should be thin)
sourceParagraphs.218: High-risk patients (obesity, unopposed estrogen, nulliparity, diabetes)
sourceParagraphs.220: During: lithotomy position, monitor VS. Usually quick and not very painful (in the office).
sourceParagraphs.221: After: monitor for bleeding, mild cramping/spotting is normal
sourceParagraphs.222: Nothing in the vagina for 72 h (infection risk).
sourceParagraphs.223: Report heavy bleeding, fever, foul discharge
sourceParagraphs.224: Chemotherapy and fevers: fever over 100.4F is an emergency
sourceParagraphs.227: Take filgrastim to stimulate bone marrow to produce neutrophils; expect bone pain
sourceParagraphs.230: Age over 50 and black men have increased mortality rates as well
sourceParagraphs.231: Father or brother with prostate cancer
sourceParagraphs.232: Diet high in red meat and high fat dairy products
sourceParagraphs.235: Most commonly spreads to bones and lymph nodes
sourceParagraphs.236: S/S: Backache, HIP PAIN, perineal/rectal discomfort, spontaneous pathologic fractures, anemia (tumor replaces bone marrow), weight loss, weakness, nausea, oliguria
sourceParagraphs.237: Early prostate cancer often has no symptoms -> normal PSA does not rule out disease
sourceParagraphs.238: Urinary obstruction symptoms mean advanced disease
sourceParagraphs.241: Seen during AIDS=Stage 3 HIV infection = CD4 < 200
sourceParagraphs.244: SOB/dyspnea, cough, chest pain, fever → may indicate opportunistic infections.
sourceParagraphs.246: Pneumocystis Pneumonia (PCP): causes hypoxemia and dry cough -> give Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
sourceParagraphs.247: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC): causes night sweats and weight loss -> give Clarithromycin (or azithromycin) + ethambutol
sourceParagraphs.250: Start PEP as soon as possible, but no later than 72 hours (3 days) after possible exposure.
sourceParagraphs.252: PrEP: Medication taken by an HIV-negative person to prevent HIV acquisition.
sourceParagraphs.259: Strict adherence to antiretroviral medications by positive partner

corrections.title: Parkinson’s Disease — Dopamine Down · Diagnosis, rigidity, and swallowing
corrections.text: A levodopa response supports diagnosis rather than proving it. Lead-pipe and cogwheel rigidity differ. Texture changes and swallow maneuvers require an individualized SLP plan, not a universal ban on thin liquids.

corrections.title: Myasthenia Gravis · Crisis management
corrections.text: Myasthenic crisis has several triggers. Cholinergic toxicity requires airway support; atropine does not reverse muscle paralysis. Benzodiazepines are not routine crisis therapy and may worsen weakness.

corrections.title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) · Lumbar-puncture aftercare
corrections.text: Routine bed rest and forced extra fluids are not proven to prevent post-dural-puncture headache. Follow the procedure plan and assess complications.

corrections.title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) · Motor neurons and communication
corrections.text: ALS involves upper and lower motor neurons. The source’s “CAM ???” is unresolved; the communication concept is presented using the verified term AAC.

corrections.title: Meningitis · Urgent care, LP, and CSF
corrections.text: Corrected Cushing triad, selected rather than routine pre-LP imaging, urgent antibiotic timing, headache prevention, and bacterial/viral CSF patterns.

corrections.title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) · Variants and treatment
corrections.text: GBS includes axonal variants. Corticosteroids do not treat GBS itself; IVIG rates and plasma-exchange calcium replacement follow product/procedure orders.

corrections.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) · DMARD timing and infection
corrections.text: Early treatment matters, but joint destruction is not confined to 12 weeks and response is not a fixed six weeks. Drug holds are agent- and infection-specific; negative serology does not exclude RA.

corrections.title: Osteoarthritis (OA) · Inflammation and pain management
corrections.text: OA can involve local inflammation. Acetaminophen is not universally first-line; exercise and suitable NSAIDs are emphasized, and injection frequency is individualized.

corrections.title: Osteoporosis · Prevention, screening, and DXA
corrections.text: Corrected age/sex-specific calcium targets, vitamin D and hormone-therapy absolutes, guideline-specific screening, and nonoverlapping T-score boundaries.

corrections.title: Gout · Cause, fluids, and medicines
corrections.text: Gout is not caused by diet alone. Hydration follows clinical needs. Allopurinol lowers urate over time; colchicine treats flares or provides prophylaxis.

corrections.title: Ménière’s Disease · Tests and maintenance therapy
corrections.text: Audiometry and symptom criteria guide diagnosis; MRI is selected. Diuretics are an optional maintenance treatment, not a guaranteed fluid-correction cure.

corrections.title: Breast and Gynecologic Cancers · Cancer care and screening
corrections.text: Qualified dye effects, SLNB/ALND comparisons and pregnancy timing, separated screening guidelines, and corrected biopsy indications, pain, aftercare, and fever/filgrastim advice.

corrections.title: Prostate Cancer · Risk and urinary symptoms
corrections.text: Diet and testosterone associations are not presented as proven universal causes. Obstruction does not establish advanced cancer; PSA and symptoms require clinical interpretation.

corrections.title: HIV and Opportunistic Infections · OI classification and prevention
corrections.text: Neuropathy is not an OI. Added complete AIDS staging context, 28-day PEP, six-monthly PrEP, limited event-driven eligibility, and U=U; prevention counseling respects confidentiality.

scope: Preserve the supplied focus points and correct unsafe/overbroad statements. Repeated pyridostigmine timing points are combined. CAM is resolved to AAC as a clinical concept, not a verified transcription. Source exam count remains explicitly attributed rather than guaranteed.
